rules: Never transmit into a load you cannot verify (dummy load or a properly matched antenna).
Verify no active operator on the frequency before TX (listen first).
Respect per-band duty-cycle limits (§15.231 rules on 315 MHz keyfob band, EN 300 220 in EU sub-GHz).
Keep TX power at the minimum required for a research reproduction; never drive to full VGA without a specific reason.
Announce yourself: at a con, coordinate with RF Village / event RF safety before intentional TX.

technical_body.recipe: hackrf_sweep across the venue band of interest at frequent intervals. Compare against a baseline sweep taken when the environment is known-quiet. Look for new peaks, sustained bursts, and unusual duty patterns.
canonical_uses: venue-side rogue-AP detection (with a WiFi tool, not HackRF)

heuristics: Sudden broadband raise across a >5 MHz span often means an overloaded ADC (turn down the LNA/VGA first, not the antenna).
Very-clean sidelobes on a suspected transmitter often indicate a numpy-generated signal (real hardware has more phase noise + timing jitter).
Flat-topped envelopes are a dead giveaway of clipping (either at the source or your own ADC).
A DC spike that follows your tune is your own; a DC spike that stays put in the spectrogram is a genuine narrowband signal.

signs: Broadband noise floor rises across the target band (e.g. keyfob receiver's band) coincident with a keyfob press failing.
Bursty noise strictly during a keyfob press window is consistent with RollJam-style jam-record-replay.
Continuous jamming often has audible tell in an FM demodulator — a constant hiss without modulation.

technical_body.note: ADS-B has no authentication; airborne integrity is enforced by SSR cross-check, ground radar, and consistency checks in ground receivers.
technical_body.hackrf_role_hint: corpus documents that TX is BLOCKED; assessments of ADS-B integrity in a venue are RX-only correlations of positions across multiple receiver stations.

technical_body.note: Unintended RF emanation from monitors, keyboards, PCB traces, and switching power supplies can carry information. HackRF can observe some of it (e.g. van Eck reconstruction of a VGA sync).
technical_body.hackrf_role_hint: the corpus mentions the concept for situational awareness; TEMPEST-grade attack pipelines are out of scope.

technical_body.note: The HackRF's maximum TX power varies by band (higher below 2 GHz, lower above). Multiply by the antenna gain (dBi) to estimate EIRP for regulatory checks.
technical_body.guideline: For §15.231 keyfob-band testing, aim well below the 60 dBuV/m at 3 m (~15 nW EIRP) limit; the HackRF at max VGA already blows past it.

name: Jamming is not documented as a canned attack

technical_body.policy: The corpus documents that jamming is technically possible with a HackRF and is illegal without authorization in most jurisdictions. No canned jamming recipe ships with this corpus. RollJam is described as historical research; its practical variant requires jamming + capture, which the corpus does not ship.

name: GPS spoofing is out of scope

technical_body.policy: GPS L1/L2/L5 TX is BLOCKED at the safety gate. Research papers on GPS spoofing (Humphreys 2012) are cited in bibliography for reference; the corpus does not ship an attack pipeline.

118-137 MHz AM voice, 1030 MHz interrogator, 1090 MHz Mode S — every aviation band is BLOCKED for TX at the safety gate. The RiskAssessor table in RiskAssessor.py is authoritative; this record is documentation only.
